newsitem.title: UK: Tradepoint secures IDB deal, hurdles remain.
newsitem.headline: Tradepoint secures IDB deal, hurdles remain.

text.p: Tradepoint, the fledgling rival of the London Stock Exchange (LSE), on Wednesday welcomed a deal with a group of inter-dealer brokers as another step towards securing its long-term survival.

As part of a 11.4 million stg refinancing first announced on Monday, Tullett & Tokyo, United Brokering and First Equity said they will report their trades on Tradepoint, Britain's first electronic trading system, because the LSE's fees were too high.
Having a majority of IDB reported bargains will make Tradepoint more attractive to the broad market, Tradepoint executive Stephen Wilson said.
"It will make Tradepoint a must have instead of nice to have, which is what we've been up until now," he said.
Yet, industry observers said the deal may not be enough to ensure the future of the two-year-old exchange.
"This deal is worse for the (London) Stock Exchange than is good for Tradepoint," said Benn Steil, head of international economics programme at the Royal Institute of International Affairs.
"All Tradepoint is doing is undercutting (the LSE). They're creating a price war for upstairs (professional) trading and Tradepoint can't possibly stay alive on upstairs trading," Steil added.

The three IDBs are part of a new group of investors in Tradepoint, which faces a fresh challenge as the LSE prepares for the October 20 launch of its own electronic trading system, which will automatically match buyers and sellers without using market-makers.

Cantor Fitzgerald, London's fourth IDB, declined to participate in the consortium because it did not find the terms of capital participation in Tradepoint attractive, said Rob Falkner, director and general council at Cantor Fitzgerald.
"But we're certainly considering membership," Falkner said. "I suspect the London Stock Exchange will react competitively and we're waiting to see who offers the best price at the moment."
A spokeswoman for the LSE said the exchange would review all aspects of its electronic trading system after its October launch, including the fee structure. She declined to elaborate.

Tradepoint has said it would break even on two percent of the LSE's turnover but has so far only attracted a fraction of that total on most days. Tradepoint's Wilson said he expects the exchange to reach its target within two years.
Wilson said IDBs, who operate between market-makers and professionals, will save 75 percent on average by reporting their bargains on Tradepoint rather than the LSE.

"Our fees would go up by 2,000 percent on October 20 under the (LSE's) proposed fee structure," said an executive with one of the major IDBs who asked not to be named. "We'd be a non-profit organisation under the (London) Stock Exchange's scheme."
"We have had extensive discussions with the Stock Exchange about pricing. We had to find an alternative," he added.
